01: At 6 p.m. Eastern, Ted Turner's Cable News Network signs on from Atlanta: the first television channel to carry news 24 hours a day.
02: Guglielmo Marconi, 22, applies for British patent 12039. It becomes the first patent for a communication system based on radio waves.
Surveyor 1 sets down in the Ocean of Storms: the first American spacecraft to soft-land on another world, four months after the Soviet Luna 9. It sends back 11,237 photographs.
03: Ed White leaves Gemini 4 for 36 minutes, steering with a hand-held oxygen jet: the first American to walk in space. Coming back in, he calls it 'the saddest moment of my life.'
04: Congress renames the Louisiana Territory the Missouri Territory, to avoid confusion with the new state of Louisiana. St. Louis is its capital; Missouri becomes a state in 1821.
In Detroit, Henry Ford takes his Quadricycle out for its first drive: a 4-horsepower, two-cylinder engine on four bicycle wheels, good for 20 mph.
Battle of Midway: six months after Pearl Harbor, American planes fatally hit the Japanese carriers Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu in a single day. The U.S. loses the carrier Yorktown.
05: Ada Lovelace, 17, meets Charles Babbage through her tutor, Mary Somerville. Later in the month he invites her to see the prototype of his difference engine.
06: Richard Hollingshead opens the first drive-in movie theater, with room for 400 cars, at Pennsauken, New Jersey. His slogan: the whole family is welcome, however noisy the children.
D-Day: 156,000 Allied soldiers land on five Normandy beaches - Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword - from nearly 7,000 vessels. It is the largest seaborne invasion in history.
07: The Edmund Fitzgerald is launched sideways at River Rouge, Michigan, before more than 15,000 people. At 729 feet she is the largest ship on the Great Lakes. The champagne bottle takes three tries.
08: An F5 tornado crosses Burnett's Mound, which legend said would shield the city, and cuts 22 miles through Topeka, Kansas, destroying 820 homes: the costliest U.S. tornado to that time.
09: Storms stall over the Black Hills of South Dakota and drop 15 inches of rain in about six hours. Rapid Creek floods Rapid City overnight; 238 people die.
10: The Great Northern Railway inaugurates the Empire Builder, named for its founder, James J. Hill. Amtrak still runs the train every day between Chicago and Seattle or Portland.
The first Apple II computers go on sale. Designed by Steve Wozniak around a 6502 processor, with color graphics, it costs $1,298 with 4 KB of memory.
11: The Paris-Bordeaux-Paris race starts: 732 miles. Emile Levassor drives the whole way himself in 48 hours 48 minutes, about 15 mph, but his two-seater is ineligible for first prize.
12: Bryan Allen pedals the Gossamer Albatross, a 70-pound aircraft designed by Paul MacCready's team, 22 miles across the English Channel in 2 hours 49 minutes on leg power alone.
13: A week after D-Day, Germany launches its first V-1 flying bombs against London. The Allies call them buzz bombs or doodlebugs; 10,492 will be launched at Britain.
Pioneer 10, launched in 1972, crosses the orbit of Neptune: the first human-made object to pass beyond the orbits of the major planets. Its last signal is received in 2003.
14: The Census Bureau dedicates the first UNIVAC I, designed principally by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. It has 6,103 vacuum tubes and weighs 16,686 pounds; 46 are built.
15: The New York Central's 20th Century Limited makes its first run, New York to Chicago in 20 hours. Passengers board along a crimson carpet: the origin of 'red-carpet treatment.'
The excursion steamer General Slocum catches fire in New York's East River with a church picnic aboard. Rotten life preservers and fire hose fail; an estimated 1,021 of 1,342 aboard die.
16: Ford Motor Company is incorporated in Detroit with $28,000 in cash from twelve investors.
Valentina Tereshkova, a textile worker and amateur parachutist, is launched in Vostok 6: the first woman in space. She makes 48 orbits in a flight of 70.8 hours.
17: Battle of Boonville: Nathaniel Lyon's Union troops, brought up the Missouri River by steamboat, scatter the Missouri State Guard in about 20 minutes. Federal control of the river is never broken.
18: Challenger lifts off on STS-7 with mission specialist Sally Ride aboard: the first American woman in space. The crew of five is the largest yet flown in one spacecraft.
19: President Roosevelt signs the Communications Act of 1934, replacing the Federal Radio Commission with the Federal Communications Commission.
20: Samuel Morse is issued U.S. patent 1,647, 'Telegraph Signs', for communicating information by signals by the application of electro-magnetism.
CBS airs the first 'Toast of the Town', hosted by Ed Sullivan. Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis perform; Rodgers and Hammerstein preview South Pacific. The show runs until 1971.
21: In Manchester, England, the 'Baby' runs its first program: 17 instructions and 52 minutes to find the highest proper divisor of 262,144. It is the first electronic stored-program computer.
Mike Melvill flies SpaceShipOne, built by Burt Rutan's Scaled Composites, from Mojave, California, to 328,491 feet: the first privately funded human spaceflight.
22: Near Hammond, Indiana, an empty troop train whose engineer has fallen asleep rams the Hagenbeck-Wallace Circus train at about 4 a.m. The wooden cars burn; 86 die and 127 are hurt.
Germany invades the Soviet Union: more than 3.8 million Axis troops on an 1,800-mile front. Operation Barbarossa becomes the largest and costliest military offensive in history.
23: Alan Turing is born in Maida Vale, London. He finishes his paper 'On Computable Numbers' in 1936; in the war he leads Hut 8 at Bletchley Park, the section working on German naval codes.
24: A British Airways 747 flies into ash from the volcano Galunggung, south of Java, and all four engines stop. The crew glides down from 37,000 feet, restarts them and lands at Jakarta. All 263 survive.
25: Lucien B. Smith of Kent, Ohio, is issued U.S. patent 66,182, 'Wire fence': the first American patent for barbed wire. Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, patents the modern kind in 1874.
CBS airs the variety special 'Premiere' in color over five East Coast stations. Black-and-white sets cannot show it and only a few dozen color sets exist; CBS drops its system in October.
26: Queen Elizabeth II and President Eisenhower formally open the St. Lawrence Seaway at Saint-Lambert, Quebec. Its 15 locks let ocean ships sail from the Atlantic into the Great Lakes.
At 8:01 a.m. in a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, 67 cents, becomes the first product rung up at a checkout by scanning its UPC bar code.
27: Joshua Slocum sails the 37-foot sloop Spray into Newport, Rhode Island, three years and more than 46,000 miles after leaving Boston: the first person to sail around the world alone.
Hurricane Audrey comes ashore near the Texas-Louisiana line with 125 mph winds and a surge of up to 12 feet. At least 416 people die, 371 of them in and around Cameron, Louisiana.
Barclays Bank in Enfield, London, installs the world's first cash machine, invented by John Shepherd-Barron. Customers feed it a paper voucher and a PIN; the limit is 10 pounds.
28: Benz & Cie. and Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft formally merge as Daimler-Benz AG, two years after agreeing to work together. Their cars will carry the name Mercedes-Benz.
29: President Eisenhower signs the Federal-Aid Highway Act: 41,000 miles of Interstate highways, $25 billion over 10 years, 90 percent federally paid. No American public works project had been larger.
The first iPhone goes on sale in the United States, announced that January: $499 with 4 GB or $599 with 8 GB, on a two-year AT&T contract. 270,000 are sold in the first week.
30: A meteor explodes in the air over Tunguska in Siberia, flattening about 830 square miles of forest. June 30 is now kept as Asteroid Day.
The first production Corvettes are built by hand in an old truck plant in Flint, Michigan: 300 that year, all white with red interiors and fiberglass bodies. In 1954 production moves to St. Louis.
